::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Pointwise linear regression and spatial teleconnection maps share the exact same math: **standardized covariance**. Whether you regress June station temperature $T$ onto June surface pressure $P$ at one location or correlate every grid cell of global sea-level pressure (SLP) against a Darwin reference series, both measure how tightly two anomalies co-vary relative to their spread. Mapping that correlation across a longitude-latitude grid turns a 1D regression into the classic **Southern Oscillation** dipole.
:::

## 1. From station regression to correlation

At a single weather station, ordinary least squares (OLS) models temperature $T_i$ as a linear function of pressure $P_i$:

$$\hat{T}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 P_i, \qquad \hat{\beta}_1 = \frac{\sum_i (P_i - \bar{P})(T_i - \bar{T})}{\sum_i (P_i - \bar{P})^2} = r_{PT} \frac{s_T}{s_P}$$

where $r_{PT}$ is the Pearson correlation coefficient and $s_T, s_P$ are the sample standard deviations. Thus, $r^2$ gives the fraction of temperature variance explained linearly by pressure, while $\hat{\beta}_1$ rescales $r_{PT}$ into physical units ($^\circ\text{C hPa}^{-1}$).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## View R code: fitting and diagnosing station temperature vs. pressure

```r
# Fit OLS: June temperature (t) vs. June pressure (p)
fit <- lm(t ~ p, data = df)
summary(fit)

# Residual diagnostics and 95% confidence interval for a new pressure reading
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(fit)

predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(p = 1012), interval = "confidence")
```
:::

## 2. Scaling up to spatial SLP teleconnection maps

Instead of correlating two scalar time series at one station, take a reference index $I(t)$—such as monthly SLP anomalies near **Darwin, Australia** ($12.4^\circ\text{S}, 130.9^\circ\text{E}$)—and compute the Pearson correlation $r(\lambda, \phi)$ at every grid point $(\lambda, \phi)$ of a global SLP field $\text{SLP}(\lambda, \phi, t)$:

$$r(\lambda, \phi) = \frac{\sum_t \big(\text{SLP}(\lambda, \phi, t) - \overline{\text{SLP}}(\lambda, \phi)\big)\big(I(t) - \bar{I}\big)}{\sqrt{\sum_t \big(\text{SLP}(\lambda, \phi, t) - \overline{\text{SLP}}(\lambda, \phi)\big)^2 \sum_t \big(I(t) - \bar{I}\big)^2}}$$

Positive correlations over the western Pacific / Indian Ocean and negative correlations over the eastern tropical Pacific (Tahiti) reveal the **Southern Oscillation** seesaw—the atmospheric half of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## View Python (`xarray`) code: computing a Darwin SLP correlation map

```python
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset("slp_1948-2014.nc")
slp = ds["slp"]  # dims: (time, lat, lon)

# Climatological mean SLP
slp_mean = slp.mean(dim="time")

# Darwin reference series (approx 12.5S, 130E)
darwin = slp.sel(lat=-12.5, lon=130.0, method="nearest")

# Grid-point correlation map
corr_map = xr.corr(slp, darwin, dim="time")
```
:::

## Key takeaways

- OLS slope $\hat{\beta}_1 = r (s_y / s_x)$ is correlation scaled by the ratio of standard deviations.
- A spatial teleconnection map applies that same pointwise correlation across every $(\lambda, \phi)$ cell against a reference index like Darwin SLP.
- Always check residual plots (linearity, homoscedasticity, autocorrelation) when interpreting climate regressions over multi-decade time series.
